sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Slightly above normal temperatures through the week.
- A slight chance of showers north of Baker to McCall on Thursday.
- Above normal temperatures and dry over the weekend into early next week. Stagnant conditions in the lower valleys with temperature inversions possible.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A weak system will pass by to the north on Thursday bringing a slight chance of showers to the west central ID mountains, with increased clouds elsewhere. Otherwise, quiet conditions as a dirty ridge develops on Friday into the weekend with high clouds and slightly warmer temperatures.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The long-term period will feature a largely stagnant pattern of broad ridging over the central CONUS and a trough off of the Pacific Northwest coast. This pattern will keep our area dry with moisture pushed to the north and support temperatures up to 10 degrees above normal. Breezy winds will develop this weekend as a short-wave clips our area, although the only other tangible evidence will be increased cloud cover. Multi-run ensemble means hint at a return to unsettled conditions after mid-week next week; although there is still considerable uncertainty in the details.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: If you like temperatures in the 60s or low 70s with sunny skies and light winds, you will enjoy Saturday through the middle of next week if you live at lower elevations.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Precipitation is moving into Park County and southern Summit and Jefferson Counties as of late this afternoon. Precipitation will continue in these areas through tonight with snow falling mainly above 7,500 feet. Snowfall amounts of 2-8" expected with isolated higher amounts possible.
- The highest snowfall amounts and worst road conditions are expected for western Park County, possibly extending into northern Park County.
- Pleasant temperatures and dry conditions are expected Thursday through early next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Water vapor imagery shows a cutoff shortwave trough just south of Grand Junction this afternoon. This trough has plenty of instability associated with it since there are numerous thunderstorms across western Colorado and eastern Utah. Meanwhile, there has been plenty of sunshine across our forecast area as the high cloud cover previously anticipated never fully developed. Some weak instability has developed over and near South Park with the SPC mesoanalysis page showing 250 j/kg of surface CAPE and mid level lapse rates peaking at 8.5 C/km. As the forcing from PVA ahead of the trough moves closer to Park County, showers and perhaps a couple of storms will form late this afternoon. Compared to model run yesterday, this system will track a bit further south. As a result, the vast majority of the precipitation will stay south of I-70 with minimal amounts, perhaps a trace to 2" of snow, forecast near the Eisenhower Tunnel. Conditions still look prime for moderate to briefly heavy snow in western and southern Park County with forecast amounts between 2-8" with higher amounts in the Mosquito Range. The Winter Weather Advisory is in effect for those areas but it is important to note that there are areas in the advisory, the I-70 corridor and northward, that will see little to no impacts from this system. Some showers may extend onto the Palmer Divide but the area of precipitation on the plains will be very minimal. PoPs and QPF were decreased across the southwestern Denver metro and anything north of I-70.
There will be brief ridging that moves over Colorado on Thursday which will lead to dry conditions and seasonal temperatures.

By Friday, a weak trough with a northerly jet behind it will bring some weak forcing to the mountains of our forecast area. There may be some light snow with amounts staying under 2" in the mountains and no snow below that.

If you like temperatures in the 60s or low 70s with sunny skies and light winds, you will enjoy Saturday through the middle of next week if you live at lower elevations. The bad news is there is almost no chance for mountain snowfall Saturday through Wednesday and that will hurt the already limited snowpack in the mountains. It's not until the 3rd week of November when models are indicating potential for more widespread precipitation across Colorado.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Monday-Wednesday...Dry west northwest flow aloft prevails with a few shortwave troughs aloft passing by, though with minimal low and mid level moisture, no precipitation expected. High temperatures nearly the same each day based on 700 mb temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near average temperatures and mostly dry conditions are expected through the rest of the work week.
- Warmer temperatures are expected to return this weekend with largely dry weather continuing.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Today, Our portion of the Intermountain West is in between two low pressure systems. There is an area of high pressure that spans across Montana that is forming a Rex block preventing the low pressure system that is moving through Utah and Colorado from taking a more northern track into our area. Mid to low level cloud cover will be moving through our area tonight. This will keep our overnight temperatures around 30 degrees tonight for the low elevations and around 25 degrees for Rawlins and Laramie. 700mb temperatures rise slightly tomorrow (from -2C to 0/1C). The surface temperatures will be a touch warmer but generally unnoticeable when compared to today. The upper level ridge will start to clear out the clouds Thursday morning but the clouds will move back in Thursday night with the next approaching short wave.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Friday...A slow moving shortwave trough aloft sweeps from western Wyoming in the morning, to eastern Wyoming by evening, spawning a slight chance of showers for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges and southern Laramie Valley, with dry conditions elsewhere. Cooler temperatures for most locations due to an increase in cloud cover and a passing weak cold front.
Saturday...Will see a slow warming trend though tempered by northerly flow aloft. Low and mid levels look too dry for any precipitation.

Sunday...The warming trend continues as the ridge aloft builds across our counties, helping to produce a surface lee trough across eastern Wyoming. 700 mb temperatures near 7 Celsius will yield maximum temperatures from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

Monday-Wednesday...Dry west northwest flow aloft prevails with a few shortwave troughs aloft passing by, though with minimal low and mid level moisture, no precipitation expected. High temperatures nearly the same each day based on 700 mb temperatures.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Beyond Thursday morning, the forecast overall looks to trend much drier. A quick moving shortwave skirts the region across the north on Friday which could bring some increased clouds and a few light rain or snow showers over the Divide.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Rivers and other waterways across southwest Colorado and southeast Utah remain elevated due to runoff. A few Flood Warnings remain in effect for those impacted areas.

- Valley rain and mountain snow will continue through late tonight and early tomorrow morning, respectively. 4 to 8 inches of snow is expected above 10,000 feet across parts of the central Colorado mountains where a Winter Weather Advisory has been issued.
- Warmer and drier conditions highlight the remainder of the seven-day forecast.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A fast moving low pressure system currently centered over eastern Utah will bring rain and mountain snow to our region through very early tomorrow morning. Rivers in southwest Colorado and southeast Utah that have continued flooding concerns from the recent prolonged rainfall event, such as the San Juan River, the Mancos River, and the Los Pinos River, are not expected to be impacted much if at all from today's rainfall as even high end (1 in 10 chance) forecasts have the liquid precipitation at or below 0.3 inches in the Four Corners area. However, there is potential for stronger convection, particularly along the Utah/Colorado border, that does increase concerns for localized flash flooding. Especially if storms producing heavier rainfall develop over flood-prone or already saturated areas.

Snowfall is expected through very early tomorrow morning, with the strongest snowfall rates forecast to occur this evening over the central Colorado mountains. A Winter Weather Advisory remains in effect this afternoon through 5 AM tomorrow morning for a portion of Colorado's central mountains, including the Gore and Elk Mountains, above 10,000 feet for 4 to 8 inches of snow. Snow levels are forecast to drop to around 7,000 feet tonight, but accumulations below 10,000 feet are expected to only be around 1 to 4 inches. Use caution if traveling as hazardous conditions could develop.

Beyond Thursday morning, the forecast overall looks to trend much drier. A quick moving shortwave skirts the region across the north on Friday which could bring some increased clouds and a few light rain or snow showers over the Divide. A broad ridge of high pressure moves in late this week into the coming weekend, with temperatures warming to above seasonable levels and providing a much needed break from the recent wet weather.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Moving into this weekend, we will enter a ridging pattern, with temperatures slightly above average, with mostly sunny conditions and light winds. The next chance of widespread rain looks to be, at the earliest, Wednesday of next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Quick-moving disturbance to bring snow to the mountains this afternoon and evening, which will make for slick and hazardous travel.
- Drier and warmer conditions starting Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Temporary ridging across the state is allowing for plenty of sun and a pleasant day across much of southern CO. Temps as of 11 AM have warmed into the 40s for the high valleys and 50s for the plains, and are expected to climb another 5 to 10 degrees through the afternoon. A closed upper low was quickly pushing across UT and will be the next weather maker for the region.

Tonight through Thursday morning...Quick-moving upper low will create a wide range of weather on the front end of the forecast. The upper low centroid pushes into western CO this afternoon, then slides to the east-southeast through the evening, then eventually moves across the SE corner of the state through the morning. This latest solution places the upper low slightly further south than previously thought, which shifts the focus out of El Paso County and moreso to the Walsenburg/Trinidad/Raton Pass area. What this translates to is a quick blast of snow across the mts tonight, with the greatest amounts expected over the central mts. A Winter Weather Advisory is in place for the higher peaks of Lake and Chaffee counties, along with Pikes Peak, for 4 to 9 inches of new snow along with some isolated higher amounts up to 11 inches, through 5 AM tomorrow morning. In addition, rest of the area will likely see some showers as well as isolated thunderstorms late this afternoon and evening as a cold front dives south across the eastern plains. The main threats from storms will be cloud to ground lightning and wind gusts as high as 45 mph, but the cold front itself will bring gusty northerly winds 30 to 35 mph. Finally, there is the chance of an hour or two of snowfall over Monument Hill, mainly between 10 PM and midnight as snow levels fall tonight, that could create reduced visibilities and slower travel conditions. However, feel that the ground is still warm enough and no accumulation is anticipated at this time.
Again, this system is moving incredibly fast which multiple model runs support, so deteriorating conditions will be short-lived.

Thursday afternoon and evening...Upper trough continues pushing to the east-southeast through the afternoon, into the central US plains, allowing for improving conditions and an end to lingering showers over the southeast corner. Gusty northerly winds through the morning will be on the wane as well. Plan on plenty of sun through the afternoon and mostly clear skies skies at night, though cloud cover will be on the increase from the west late. Look for highs in the mid 40s to lower 50s for the high valleys, and 50s to around 60F for the plains. Overnight low temps will drop into the 20s for the high valleys, and 30s for the plains. Moore

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: By Friday, the band of elevated 500mb vorticity, should have filtered out of the area, leaving us with ridging aloft. It may be possible for westerly flow, combined with modest humidity, to produce orographic precipitation on the windward side of the higher terrain, especially the central mountains, in the afternoon. For the rest of the area, expect a dry, partly cloudy day.

Moving into this weekend, we will enter a ridging pattern, with temperatures slightly above average, with mostly sunny conditions and light winds. The next chance of widespread rain looks to be, at the earliest, Wednesday of next week.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: High pressure will build heading into the weekend, resulting in a steady warming trend that will bring temperatures closer to 5-10 degrees above normal by early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A weak system traverses the Great Basin today, bringing light valley rain and high elevation snowfall to northern and central Utah.
- A second weak storm system may graze northern Utah on Friday before high pressure builds for the weekend, keeping temperatures around 5 degrees below normal.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Morning satellite imagery reveals an apparent circulation shifting across Utah, associated with a mid-level closed low that brought scattered light showers to the area. As this low continues to track eastward, these showers will do the same, largely ending by midnight tonight. Low-level clouds are likely to linger into the morning hours across much of the area, potentially inhibiting fog potential even for fog-prone locations such as the Cache Valley.

A weak shortwave trough moving through the area late Thursday night/early Friday morning is trending stronger with recent model runs, though moisture will be very limited, even moreso than today. Still, isolated showers may develop across far northeastern Utah/southwest Wyoming Thursday night; sometimes, a vort max will provide enough lift to produce showers despite this lack of moisture. Increased cloud cover, alongside slightly better mixing, may once again inhibit valley fog development early Friday morning, something that looked more likely in prior forecasts. Finally, this wave will also act to keep temperatures around 5 degrees below normal through Friday.

High pressure will build heading into the weekend, resulting in a steady warming trend that will bring temperatures closer to 5-10 degrees above normal by early next week. Forecast confidence is low in our next precipitation chances; model guidance suggests a return as early as next Thursday, but likely not until Friday or later.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You could trigger an avalanche in wind-drifted snow above treeline that could be large enough to bury you.

The most dangerous slopes are where recent winds drifted snow into thicker, stiffer slabs on steep slopes above 12,000 feet. Look for and avoid wind-buffed snow surfaces and pillowy drifts in cross-loaded couloirs, rocky windward slopes, and lee slopes directly below ridgelines.
Safer travel options exist in wind-sheltered areas at lower elevations.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. Steer around steep slopes near ridgelines with continuous, firm snow cover. You might find these slopes at high elevations.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Spencer Logan
bottom_line: Fresh snow means you could trigger avalanches above treeline. Look for and avoid spots where winds drift the new snow. Those spots will be just below ridgelines, along gully walls, or around terrain features like rock outcrops. Because wind speeds with this storm are light, the drifted snow may be softer and less obvious than the typical Colorado wind slab. Most slopes near and below treeline lack enough snow to produce an avalanche.
